newsitem.title: FRANCE: Even on roadblocks, French find truckers "sympa".
newsitem.headline: Even on roadblocks, French find truckers "sympa".

text.p: For decades, France's most popular late-night radio show was called "Les routiers sont sympas" (Truckers are nice), a slogan millions of motorists displayed on cheerful bumper-stickers.

That may explain why, far from provoking public anger by barricading motorways and blockading fuel depots across the provinces, French truck drivers have recaptured a popularity they do not always enjoy with fellow road users.

An opinion poll taken for France 2 public television showed that 74 percent of the public support the truckers' nine-day-old strike, 87 percent think their demands are justified and 59 percent back their tactics of blocking the nation's highways.

Exploited truck drivers trying to force rogue bosses to respect accords on working conditions signed in 1994 but widely flouted have become this year's working-class heroes, just as railmen were during last year's 24-day public transport strike.

Newspapers from the Communist left to the conservative right have depicted the drivers as "les forcats de la route" (slaves of the roads), forced by their employers to overwork, break speed limits and take risks to meet inhuman delivery deadlines.
Analysts say this public sympathy is partly due to France's revolutionary tradition of taking grievances into the streets.
It mirrors the record unpopularity of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right government and its austerity policies.
But it also reflects widespread anxiety about the increasing pressures of the global economy and its cut-throat competition, of which the truck drivers are seen as victims.

The newspaper Le Monde said the truckers' harsh working conditions are the direct result of government policies that have long given preference to transporting goods by road rather than by rail or canal.

If road hauliers respected French labour laws and safety regulations, the cost of transporting goods would be 20 percent higher, according to estimates by the National Accounts Commission and the state planning commissioner.

Instead, truckers complain they are often forced by their bosses to fiddle the "spy in the cab" tachograph, which records their mileage, driving time and rest breaks, and to ignore speed limits to make deliveries on time.

According to official figures, France has 225,000 full-time salaried drivers, of whom 174,000 transport goods and 49,000 carry passengers. Their average working week in 1993 was 62.5 hours, well beyond the European Union legal maximum of 48 hours.
Most drivers work for small firms employing fewer than 10 staff, giving them less protection than employees of big firms.

While French motorists often grumble at truck drivers thundering along the nation's highways at speeds that bear no relation to the limits displayed on obligatory stickers, most sympathise with their spartan way of life.
Many drivers can only make ends meet by sleeping in their cabs and eating at "Les Routiers" restaurants that dot French highways, offer special low-price menus for truckers.

Farmers in the southwestern town of Sainte-Foye-la-Grande, near Bordeaux, cooked a giant barbacue for striking truckers manning a nearby roadblock last weekend. The nearby town of Cahors opened a disused school to enable strikers to have a wash and shave.
Elsewhere, local residents have contributed firewood to help picketing drivers keep warm through freezing November nights.
